p: After the young Anteo Zamboni tried to assassinate Benito Mussolini in Bologna on 31 October 1926, the Italian government quickly passed repressive laws. All parties and associations opposed to the regime were dissolved. On 25 November 1926 the State Defence Law set up a Special Court to try those accused of being enemies of the state and restored the death penalty. The public security code enacted in 1926 specified a department of political police as a special division of the force. Its existence stayed secret until December 1930, when the official press agency Agenzia Stefani named the OVRA as a special section of the police.

Arturo Bocchini appointed the inspector Francesco Nudi as head of the OVRA; he was later replaced by Guido Leto. The organisation compiled files on around 130,000 potential subversives with the aid of approximately 100,000 informants, and by 1930 it was organising around 20,000 raids each week. About 6,000 of those it arrested, mainly communists and members of Giustizia e Libertà, are believed to have been tried by the Special Court or exiled to remote Mediterranean islands, where conditions were extremely poor. It also kept the Casellario Politico Centrale, an archive of personal profiles of known subversives.

The OVRA spied on Pope Pius XI, blackmailing priests into informing; the historian David Kertzer described its network in the Vatican as robust. Heinrich Himmler met Bocchini repeatedly, and the two police forces signed a secret protocol of cooperation on 2 April 1936. During the Second World War the OVRA was used against resistance groups in the Balkans, and in 1943 it tried to infiltrate the British Special Operations Executive with double agents. Many agents followed Mussolini to the Italian Social Republic, where they were favoured targets of communist partisans.

The OVRA was officially disbanded after the war, but a decree of 26 April 1945 ordered that the central political archive be maintained. A new police division, the Servizio Informazioni Speciali, took over its management, and many former OVRA officers were reinstated in it; its head, Inspector General Santoro, had been one of Leto's deputies. Most of the public security laws of 1931 were kept in force by the Italian Republic, and Leto himself was later reinstated as a police officer and put in charge of supervising the police academies.

notes: The article's figures do not agree: the lead says 'approximately 50,000 OVRA agents', the body 'a network of approximately 100,000 informants'. I used the body's figure only.

The article names several Vatican clerics and repeats allegations about their sexual conduct from Kertzer; I left the names and allegations out and kept only that priests were blackmailed into informing.
The article claims Himmler modelled the Nazi secret police on the OVRA; I kept only the meetings and the 1936 protocol.
